title: Straight Up
subtitle: Sea level to the edge of space
sourceNote: The Karman line at 100 km is the FAI's conventional boundary of space, not a physical edge — the atmosphere just keeps thinning.

waypoints.name: The top of the tallest building
waypoints.body: The Burj Khalifa, 828 metres. The tallest thing humans have ever built, and you are not even one percent of the way up.

waypoints.name: Where altitude sickness starts
waypoints.body: Above about 2,500 metres the thinner air starts to affect most people. Roughly two percent of the way to space.

waypoints.name: Half the atmosphere is below you
waypoints.body: Half of all the air on Earth, by mass, is now beneath your feet. You are five percent of the way to the edge.

waypoints.name: The summit of Everest
waypoints.body: The highest anyone stands without a machine. A third of the oxygen of sea level, and still under nine percent of the way up.

waypoints.name: Cruising altitude
waypoints.body: Where airliners fly, just below the tropopause. Outside it is around minus fifty-five degrees.

waypoints.name: The Armstrong limit
waypoints.body: Above this the pressure is so low that the water in your body boils at its own temperature. A pressure suit stops being optional.

waypoints.name: The ozone layer
waypoints.body: A thin band of gas absorbing most of the Sun's ultraviolet. Compressed to sea-level pressure it would be about three millimetres thick.

waypoints.name: The highest skydive
waypoints.body: Felix Baumgartner stepped off a balloon here in 2012 and fell for four minutes, breaking the sound barrier on the way down.

waypoints.name: The stratopause
waypoints.body: Halfway. The top of the stratosphere, where the air stops warming with height and starts cooling again.

waypoints.name: The mesopause
waypoints.body: About minus ninety degrees, the coldest place anywhere on Earth. Noctilucent clouds form here, made of ice on meteor dust.

waypoints.name: The Karman line
waypoints.body: Officially space. The air is still there, just far too thin to fly in — from here you have to orbit instead.
